paper_title: It Takes Workflows to Evolve Better Workflows

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Tackling complex real-world tasks can exceed the capabilities of a single large language model (LLM), motivating the use of multi-agent workflows that coordinate specialized agents to work together on these tasks. Recent methods train LLMs to construct better workflows from execution outcomes, but they optimize only the workflow generator, while the other agents that build or execute each workflow remain fixed even though every outcome depends on all of them. However, extending training beyond the generator is challenging: the agents are coupled, and a workflow's outcome is a single sparse score that cannot tell which agent causes a failure. We propose FloWright, which leverages the workflow as a harness to optimize workflows. By introducing a hierarchical, structure-aware reward paradigm, FloWright enables one role to self-evolve and two or more roles to co-evolve, with no additional models, labels, or executions. Considering the limitation that workflows are commonly trained and evaluated on data that a single agent can already handle, we further propose DataWright, an adaptive data hardening approach that converts existing datasets into workflow-level tasks with increased difficulty. Across document, slide, chart, code, math, and finance tasks, small open models trained with FloWright achieve improved performance by up to $+7.41\%$, with co-evolving ($+5.03\%$) more roles gaining more than optimizing one of them alone ($+2.83\%$). Our project page: https://xhguo7.github.io/FloWright/.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly capable of leveraging tools and specialized skills to solve tasks (Zhang et al., 2025e; Qian et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025c; Zhang et al., 2026a). However, tackling complex real-world problems can go beyond the capability of single LLM, as it demands gathering evidence across heterogeneous inputs, reasoning over long contexts and diverse sources, and accumulating intermediate results over many steps (Yu et al., 2025b; Zhu et al., 2025). To address such tasks, LLMs construct multi-agent workflows that break complex tasks into subtasks and coordinate specialized agents (Zhang et al., 2025d; Hu et al., 2025b; Niu et al., 2025). Yet constructing an effective workflow for complex task remains challenging, and many multi-agent frameworks still rely on substantial manual design (Jin et al., 2026; Li et al., 2025; Agashe et al., 2025). To reduce this manual effort, recent works optimize LLMs to construct better workflows by training them against the outcomes of executing those workflows (Nie et al., 2025; Nielsen et al., 2026). However, these methods typically optimize single workflow generator, while the agents that execute the workflow, and any other agents that help build it, remain fixed (A.1). Since the outcome of workflow depends jointly on every agent that builds or executes it, training only the generator leaves other agents shaping every outcome without ever learning from it, significantly limiting how much the workflow as whole can improve. Extending training beyond the generator introduces two additional challenges. First, agents in workflow are interdependent: one agents output can become anothers input, and overall performance depends on their joint behavior Existing multi-agent training either trains each agent separately (Guo et al., 2026; Motwani et al., 2025) or co-trains agents with distinct roles only within fixed pairing or hand-designed system (Park et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026; Wan et al., 2025) (A.2). Training agents separately thus ignores how each agents behavior shapes what the others learn, while co-training remains confined to single role or predefined agent structure rather than the workflows constructed for each task. Second, the outcome of workflow is usually single score for the whole workflow. It is sparse whenever the workflow falls short, and cannot tell which agent Equal co-mentorship. Correspondence: Xuehang Guo <xguo15@wm.edu>, Zhenhailong Wang <wangz3@illinois.edu>, Qingyun Wang <qwang16@wm.edu> 1 FLOWRIGHT: It Takes Workflows to Evolve Better Workflows causes failure. Methods that do attribute failures to specific agents or steps, however, rely heavily on learned critics or reward models, LLM judges, human annotation, or repeated executions (Liu et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025b; Ma et al., 2026) (A.3). Such attribution adds costly models, labels, or executions beyond the workflow run itself, and it can still misattribute where failure originates. Beyond how workflows are built and trained, the data used to optimize and evaluate them pose further challenge. Multi-agent workflows are commonly trained and evaluated on datasets such as single-question math, function-level coding, and short question answering, which single agent can already handle (Zhang et al., 2026b) (A.4). On such data, re-evaluations find that the gains of multi-agent systems over strong single agent are often small or absent (Cemri et al., 2025; Choi et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2026) (C). These datasets can therefore neither reveal nor optimize what workflow adds beyond single agent. Motivated by these limitations, we propose FLOWRIGHT (3), which leverages the workflow as harness (2) to optimize any role (3.5). Besides letting each role self-evolve, FLOWRIGHT co-evolves multiple roles inside the harness (3.4), and stages the grade into hierarchical, structureaware reward (3.3) with role-level credit localization (3.2). Beyond workflow construction and optimization, FLOWRIGHT introduces data adaptation algorithm (Alg. 1) that hardens existing datasets for workflow-level training and evaluation (D). Our contributions are as follows: 1 Shared harness for every role, at train and test time. We define shared workflow harness whose signal serves three purposes (2.1): the evaluation metric (D.4), the optimization signal for training any role  (Fig. 2)  , and the meta distillation objective at test time (3.5). 2 Structure-aware credit at no extra cost. We design reward hierarchy that turns the sparse signal of workflow into dense, role-level feedback (3.3), with credit read from the execution trace that the harness already records, requiring no additional models, labels, or executions (3.2). 3 Workflow-level data hardening. We propose DATAWRIGHT, data adaptation approach whose three hardening strategies convert datasets single agent can already handle into workflow-level tasks with increased difficulty levels, supporting both training and evaluation (D). 4 Four evolution modes that generalize. FLOWRIGHT enables four evolution modes (3.4): (a) single-role self-evolution, (b) agent-skill co-evolution, (c) upstream-downstream co-evolution, and (d) multi-agent co-evolution. Co-evolving more roles gains more than optimizing one alone, achieving +5.03% overall against +2.83% for single role (5.1). In addition, gains are generalizable across roles, backbones, RL algorithms, workflow topologies, and pools (5.2).

sections.title: 3 FLOWRIGHT: LEARNING TO WRIGHT WORKFLOWS
sections.content: For task xi , upstream produces workflow (2, 3.1). FLOWRIGHT  (Fig. 2)  grounds it into measurable optimization signal h(G, xi) through principled harness with both local crediting (3.2) and global hierarchy (3.3). By learning to optimize this signal, FLOWRIGHT enables LLMs to solve complex tasks by building better workflows, through self-evolution and co-evolution (3.4) at both train and test time (3.5).

sections.title: 3.1 WIRE THE WORKFLOW: TOPOLOGY & POOL DYNAMICS
sections.content: Upstream construction turns on three choices: the topology of the workflow G, and the granularity and dynamics of the pool Ω it draws from. Topology is non-linear control-flow graph. Beyond passing progress forward in chain, πg runs nodes in parallel when subtasks are independent, forks alternative branches that are later reconciled, and repeats step until stopping condition is met. single workflow can thus express sequential, parallel, branching, and iterative structure as the task demands. Pool is presented to the upstream at chosen granularity  (Fig. 1)  . fine, modular granularity keeps agents, tools, and skills as separate units to enable flexible selection and composition: Ω = Ωagent Ωtool Ωskill. coarse granularity bundles each agent with necessary tools and skills into self-contained capsule, leading to Ω = Ωcapsule. Pool is dynamic. When task calls for capability that Ω does not contain, the pool is expanded with the missing component, new tool, skill, or agent. The upstream thus grows its own components during construction in addition to drawing directly from the pool  (Fig. 1)  . Holding the pool static disables this growth, setting we ablate in our experiments (5.2).

sections.title: 3.3 HARNESS THE WORKFLOW: A HIERARCHICAL REWARD
sections.content: The harness does not reduce an execution to single pass-or-fail outcome. Instead, it stages the optimization signal into principled hierarchy of auto-verified terms, so the policy sees meaningful gradient even when the workflow falls short. As such, we propose our hierarchical reward as generic paradigm: one shared harness from which every optimizable role adaptively instantiates its own reward. Optimization signal is staged ladder. Reward terms accumulate from the roles own output to the task outcome: whether the roles output oρ parses (f ), whether the roles contribution is valid (vρ), whether the workflow executes to final answer (e), and how correct that answer is (a). The local credit of 3.2 enters as fifth, structure-aware term, extending the ladder across local and global. As such, the signal for role ρ is: = hρ(Gj, xi) = wf + wv vρ + we + wa + wc cρ hρ (3) where {wf , wv, we, wa, wc} are weighting coefficients configured per role (F.2). Our hierarchical ladder thus composes one optimization signal across two axes: from the roles own output to the task outcome, the staged four terms measure how far workflow reaches; from local to global, the credit term (3.2) localizes failures to roles at fault. FLOWRIGHT aims to maximize this signal at train and test time (3.4, 3.5).

sections.title: 3.4 HARNESS FOR EVOLUTION: ONE ROLE OR MUTUAL CURRICULUM
sections.content: Our reward paradigm serves every role from one shared harness, enabling one role to self-evolve or several to co-evolve. Any single role self-evolves inside the harness. To train role, we optimize its role-specific reward hρ inside the harness as it runs, so the role evolves in the same flow that will use it (4a). The same procedure fits any role, since all roles share one harness. Several roles co-evolve inside the harness through mutual curriculum. When several roles train on one substrate inside one harness, each roles behavior shapes what the others encounter. Improving one role therefore reshapes the experience the rest learn from. The co-evolving roles can thus share one policy or each keep their own, and in either case each role learns against the latest evolved policies of the others. For example, co-evolution can pair an agent with its own skill (4b), couple an upstream agent that builds the workflow with downstream agent that executes it (4c), or co-train any two or more agents (4d). In each case, the coupling is mutual curriculum: each role shapes the training distribution the others learn from. The structure-aware credit of 3.2 charges each role only for the failures of its own nodes in the shared execution, which separates the roles credit wherever their footprints differ.

sections.title: 4 EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: Setup. We evaluate FLOWRIGHT in both objectives it optimizes (3.5): reinforcement learning at train time, and meta distillation at test time. At train time, we cover four evolution modes (3.4): (a) single-role self-evolution, (b) agent-skill co-evolution, (c) upstream-downstream co-evolution, and (d) multi-agent co-evolution. We compare them against two single-agent baselines, with or without the tool and skill pools  (Fig. 1)  . Each baseline runs with the same compute budget as our FLOWRIGHT counterpart it is compared against. All evaluations are on the held-out test sets, non-overlapped with training data (D.5). sections.title: 5.1 EVOLVE THE ROLES: OPTIMIZE ANY ROLE BY HARNESSING THE WORKFLOW
sections.content: FLOWRIGHT improves performance in every regime at train time. Comparing with single-agent baselines, untrained FLOWRIGHT showcases improved performance ( +11.39% overall). This reveals that models with smaller sizes are able to build and run workflows with gains better than its size acting alone. At matched model size, every evolution mode exceeds its untrained counterpart in every regime and overall by up to +7.41% (Tab. 1), and every arm improves under at least one mode. Moreover, the gain also increases when more roles co-evolve. Multi-agent co-evolution gains +7.32% in-distribution, +6.05% out-of-distribution, and +4.20% out-of-domain, staying positive across all datasets, strategies, and levels  (Fig. 12)  . Among the four Qwen3.5-4B modes, multi-agent co-evolution leads 7/8 columns of Tab. 1 and gains most overall at +5.03%, ahead of agent-skill coevolution at +4.06%, upstream-downstream co-evolution at +3.06% and single-role self-evolution at +2.83%. These improvements indicate that co-evolving more roles yields more than optimizing one of them alone. Harnessing the workflow therefore carries what FLOWRIGHT learns on four datasets at one hardening strategy and one level to the strategies, levels, and domains held out from it. FLOWRIGHT also improves performance at test time. In place of policy parameters, FLOWRIGHT additionally distills reusable prior at test time (3.5) for improved adaptability on new tasks. Test-time and train-time optimization then compound, reaching +3.21% overall, +4.14% in-distribution, +3.80% out-ofdistribution, and +2.79% out-of-domain, exceeding the five-shot prior alone by +1.59% and leading other settings across regimes. On the other hand, for in-distribution, it stays within 0.01% of CISPO. The harness provides learning signal generalizable to different RL algorithms. Figure 4: Algorithm Generalizability. As shown in Fig. 5, grading format and answer alone stays close to the untrained baseline, with +0.07% under GRPO and +0.80% under DAPO. Adding validity reward contributes the largest single increment at +2.07% under GRPO and +2.29% under DAPO, respectively. The structure-aware credit of 3.2 adds further +0.69% and +0.75%, reaching +2.83% and +3.84% overall, respectively. Each layer of the reward ladder contributes, with validity contributing the most. sections.title: 6 RELATED WORK
sections.content: We summarize four lines of work below and extend each in A. Workflow Construction and Optimization. Early multi-agent frameworks coordinate agents through manually specified roles and procedures (Hong et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2023). Later methods automate this design while keeping every model fixed, searching for workflow writFigure 8: Pool Dynamics. static pool stays fixed, dynamic pool expands on demand, and grown pool also carries components distilled from past experiences (3.1). 8 FLOWRIGHT: It Takes Workflows to Evolve Better Workflows ten as code (Zhang et al., 2025d; Hu et al., 2025b) or generating graph for each task and revising it during execution (Niu et al., 2025), and further line trains the generator itself from execution outcomes (Zhang et al., 2025a; Nie et al., 2025; Nielsen et al., 2026). separate line improves the workflow without updating any weights, inducing reusable routines from past experience (Wang et al., 2024), evolving the context model conditions on (Zhang et al., 2026c), or replacing reinforcement learning with reflective prompt evolution (Agrawal et al., 2026). However, the models that solve the workflows subtasks remain fixed, limiting how much the workflow as whole can improve. Multi-Agent Training and Co-Evolution. Reinforcement learning increasingly optimizes several interacting agents, yet within an interaction structure fixed in advance, such as discussion among agents that play one role (Park et al., 2025) or workflow designed once per task domain (Zhao et al., 2026). Co-evolution likewise fixes how the models interact, pairing challenger that proposes problems with solver that answers them (Huang et al., 2026), or scoring proposals in multi-round discussion (Xue et al., 2026). Other works train each agent separately, in its own reinforcement learning with role-specific dataset and reward (Guo et al., 2026; Motwani et al., 2025). However, agents then learn in isolation or in one fixed role, rather than over the workflows constructed for each task. Credit Assignment and Failure Attribution. Credit finer than single outcome typically comes from learned models, such as process reward model trained alongside the policy (Liu et al., 2025) or local reward for each component, estimated by re-executing what follows it (Wu et al., 2026). Failure attribution instead names the responsible agent and step with LLM judges (Zhang et al., 2025f), an attributor trained on labeled failures (Zhang et al., 2025b), or re-execution with edited messages (Ma et al., 2026), yet identifies the decisive step in only about third of failed runs (Chen et al., 2026). Credit that adds no model or rollout compares actions taken from states that recur across single agents rollouts of the same task (Feng et al., 2025; Cheng et al., 2026). However, such attribution costs models, labels, or executions beyond the workflow run itself, and it can still misattribute where failure originates. Evaluation of Multi-Agent Workflows. Methods that construct or optimize workflows are commonly evaluated on single-question math, function-level code, and short question answering (Zhang et al., 2025d;a; Nie et al., 2025). On such data, automatically designed systems improve on self-consistent single agent by at most few points (Singh et al., 2025), and majority voting alone accounts for most of the gains attributed to multi-agent debate (Choi et al., 2025). Training on it can also collapse system into one dominant agent (Zhang et al., 2025h), and failure analyses find the reported gains often minimal (Cemri et al., 2025). However, such data can neither reveal nor optimize what workflow adds beyond single agent.

sections.title: 7 CONCLUSIONS
sections.content: In this work, we introduce FLOWRIGHT, which leverages the workflow as harness (3.1) to provide the optimization signal without additional annotations: one signal that evaluates workflow, trains any role that builds or executes it, and evolves reusable prior at test time (2.1, 3.5). hierarchical, structure-aware reward (3.3) turns the sparse outcome of workflow into role-level feedback, with role-specific credit derived from the execution trace (3.2). FLOWRIGHT enables train-time optimization in four modes: (1) single role self-evolution, (2) agent-skill co-evolution, (3) upstreamdownstream co-evolution, and (4) two or more roles co-evolve; and test-time optimization via meta distillation (3.4). To supply reliable workflow-level evaluation, we further propose DATAWRIGHT to convert single agent level datasets into workflow-level tasks through three hardening strategies at two levels, yielding the 44 arms our experiments span (D). Across those arms, FLOWRIGHT outperforms the single-agent baselines by +11.39%, adds further +2.58% through meta distillation and +5.03% through reinforcement optimization (5.1). These gains hold across RL algorithms, workflow topologies, pool granularities, and pool dynamics (5.2), and transfer to backbones the harness never trains (G.2). 9 FLOWRIGHT: It Takes Workflows to Evolve Better Workflows

sections.title: A EXTENDED DISCUSSION OF RELATED WORK
sections.content: A.1 WORKFLOW CONSTRUCTION AND OPTIMIZATION Early multi-agent frameworks coordinate agents through manually specified roles, procedures, and conversation patterns (Hong et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2023), and recent visual document understanding systems run agent pipelines designed by hand for their domain on fixed, prompted backbones (Zhu et al., 2025; Jin et al., 2026). Other methods automate this design while keeping every model fixed, searching on each benchmarks validation data for single workflow or agent design written as code (Zhang et al., 2025d; Hu et al., 2025b), or generating workflow graph for each task and revising it during execution (Niu et al., 2025). Methods that train the workflow generator use supervised fine-tuning on query-specific multi-agent systems (Ye et al., 2025) or learn from execution outcomes, training lightweight controllers that select operators (Zhang et al., 2025a) or communication edges (Zhang et al., 2025c) for fixed LLMs, weak meta-agent that designs workflows for strong executors (Nie et al., 2025), or orchestrators that assign subtasks to fixed worker models (Nielsen et al., 2026) or select the next agent step by step (Dang et al., 2025). Such training also extends to several meta-agents that generate, configure, and rectify multi-agent system whose agents run on fixed model pool (Wang et al., 2025a). separate line improves the workflow without updating weights, leveraging reusable routines from past experience (Wang et al., 2024), evolving the context model conditions on (Zhang et al., 2026c), or replacing reinforcement learning with reflective prompt evolution (Agrawal et al., 2026). However, in all these methods, the models that solve the workflows subtasks remain fixed, which limits how much the workflow as whole can improve. A.2 MULTI-AGENT TRAINING AND CO-EVOLUTION Reinforcement learning increasingly optimizes multiple interacting LLM agents, but within an interaction structure fixed in advance for all task instances, such as multi-turn discussion among agents that play the same role (Park et al., 2025), meta-thinking agent that guides reasoning agent (Wan et al., 2025), workflow designed once per task domain (Zhao et al., 2026), or document-understanding pipeline of planning, execution, judgment, and answering agents (Yu et al., 2025b). Co-evolution methods likewise fix how the models interact, pairing challenger that proposes problems with solver that answers them (Huang et al., 2026), or letting agents drawn at random propose, critique, and score solutions in multi-round discussion whose scores serve as their rewards (Xue et al., 2026). Recursive agent training lets the task decomposition vary per instance, but trains single policy as root agent and as the copies of itself to which it delegates, all in the same role (Gandhi et al., 2026). Other works train each agent separately, optimizing it in its own reinforcement learning with role-specific dataset and reward (Guo et al., 2026), or fine-tuning it to draft, verify, or refine an answer on trajectories sampled once from the untrained model (Motwani et al., 2025). However, these agents learn either in isolation or only within the one structure or role they are trained in, which leaves them unprepared for tasks whose outcome depends on different agents working together in different ways. A.3 CREDIT ASSIGNMENT AND FAILURE ATTRIBUTION Credit finer than single outcome often comes from learned models, such as process reward model trained alongside single agents policy to reward each action (Liu et al., 2025), or local reward for each component of compound system, learned from outcomes estimated by re-executing the components downstream of it (Wu et al., 2026). Other methods credit the meta-agents that design multi-agent system by averaging the outcomes of executions branched at each of their decisions (Wang et al., 2025a). Failure attribution for multi-agent systems names the responsible agent and step with LLM judges (Zhang et al., 2025f) or with an attributor trained on failures labeled through counterfactual replay and fault injection (Zhang et al., 2025b), or tests failure hypotheses by re-executing the system with edited messages or plans (Ma et al., 2026). Even with full execution traces, such attributors identify the decisive failure step in only about third of failed runs (Chen et al., 2026). Credit that adds no model or rollout instead compares actions taken from states that recur across single agents rollouts of the same task, and falls back to trajectory-level credit when states do not recur (Feng et al., 2025; Cheng et al., 2026). However, such credit either costs extra models, labels, or executions, or holds only where single agent revisits the same states, and it can 15 FLOWRIGHT: It Takes Workflows to Evolve Better Workflows still misattribute failures. Consequently, agents that share one outcome lack cheap and reliable signal of their own mistakes. A.4 EVALUATION OF MULTI-AGENT WORKFLOWS Methods that construct or optimize multi-agent workflows are commonly evaluated on single-question math, function-level code, and short question answering (Zhang et al., 2025d;a; Nie et al., 2025). On such data, automatically designed multi-agent systems improve on self-consistent single agent by at most few points (Singh et al., 2025), many reported successes of efficiency methods for multiagent systems appear in settings where single agent already preserves strong performance (Zhang et al., 2026b), and majority voting alone accounts for most of the gains attributed to multi-agent debate (Choi et al., 2025). When multiple agents are trained on single-question math, one agent comes to dominate while the other contributes little, collapsing the system into single agent (Zhang et al., 2025h). Final answer accuracy can also remain high while the interactions among agents diverge from their intended behavior (So et al., 2026), and failure analyses find the gains of multi-agent systems on popular benchmarks often minimal (Cemri et al., 2025). However, as such data can be solved without coordinating agents, evaluating on it cannot reliably assess whether workflows structure helps, and training on it provides little signal for learning beyond single agents effort.

sections.content: By proposing FLOWRIGHT, there are also limitations that confine the scope of what we demonstrate. First, our reinforcement learning experiments are mainly evaluated on two open models of single family, Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.5-9B (4). FLOWRIGHT leverages the same signal whichever model powers role, and the meta-distillation improves all four backbones we evaluate, including the two it never optimizes (G.2). Nevertheless, we aim to incorporate more model families into our evaluation to strengthen our work. Second, our evaluation spans 44 arms over 12 datasets and 7 domains (D.5), each task whose inputs are fixed once the task begins. In future work, we plan to train roles at larger scale, and to extend FLOWRIGHT to dynamic environments, where the inputs workflow reads and the components it needs change while the workflow runs. PRELIMINARY STUDY: THE GAP IN EXISTING BENCHMARKS multi-agent workflow is only warranted on task that single agent cannot already solve. We therefore ask two questions: what existing benchmarks demand of system, whether single agent or workflow, and how much workflow gains on them. We answer the first by surveying the evaluations that published workflow generation methods use, and the second by controlled comparison in which the workflow and the single agent both run the untrained backbone Qwen3-VL-8B. What Existing Benchmarks Demand. We collect every dataset that each of 20 workflow generation methods published at top-tier venues evaluates on (Zhang et al., 2025d; Hu et al., 2025b; Zhang et al., 2025a; Zhuge et al., 2024; Shang et al., 2025; Nie et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025a; Dang et al., 2025; Ke et al., 2026; Nielsen et al., 2026; Su et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2025c; Niu et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025g; Zhou et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2025b; Hu et al., 2025a; Singh et al., 2025), which gives 121 datasets in total, counting dataset once for each method that uses it. We classify these 121 datasets into six categories according to what system needs to do to answer each question (Fig. 9a): single-question math (39), short-answer QA (25), function-level coding (21), tool use or agentic environments (16), reading comprehension (4), and other (16). The first three categories account for 85 of the 121, and single competent agent is able to answer their questions in one pass 1. How Much Workflow Gains on Them. Leveraging Qwen3-VL-8B as the backbone, we compare LLM-generated multi-agent workflow against single agent on two datasets of this kind (MMLongBench-Doc (Ma et al., 2024) and DocFinQA (Reddy et al., 2025)). We give the workflow and the single agent the same compute budget, so that any difference in accuracy is attributable to how the computation is organized rather than to how much of it each system is allowed (Fig. 9b). On 1These counts describe the 20 methods we survey, and we do not extrapolate them to the field. 16 FLOWRIGHT: It Takes Workflows to Evolve Better Workflows the original MMLongBench-Doc (200-sample subset) the workflow reaches 40.50% and the single agent 48.00%. On the original DocFinQA (200-sample subset) the workflow reaches 33.00% and the single agent 38.00%. Neither dataset rewards multi-agent coordination. Each sample presents one document and one question, so system reads through the document and extracts one answer, and no decision in the task requires ability or coordination beyond single agent. The outcome therefore reflects what these benchmarks ask for, not limitation of the workflow. Hardening Changes the Outcome. On MMLongBench-Doc hardened by DATAWRIGHT, the same workflow reaches 51.61% against the single agents 12.33% over 150 test samples, an improvement of 39.28 points. Through hardening (D.1), the evidence system needs to examine exceeds one effective context window. Therefore, the task requires deciding which input to read in what order, and spending the same number of turns on single input no longer suffices. This is the condition under which the structure and coordination workflow adds carry value 2. Figure 9: Preliminary Study. DATAWRIGHT: WORKFLOW-LEVEL DATA HARDENING Datasets that single agent can already handle can neither reveal nor optimize what workflow adds beyond it (C). To this end, we propose DATAWRIGHT to convert existing datasets into workflowlevel tasks. Particularly, it builds each task by rule-based hardening strategy at hardening level ℓ (D.1), adaptively selects the strategies each dataset supports (D.2), and filters the data with quality control (D.3). Each hardened task is graded as the mean of its sub-question scores, and the accuracy of each hardened dataset is calculated as the mean accuracy over its test tasks (D.4). sections.title: LEVELS
sections.content: FLOWRIGHT improves performance across diverse datasets, hardening strategies, and task complexities. As shown in Fig. 12, the improvement holds on every dataset: under multi-agent coevolution, all 12 datasets gain over the untrained workflow, with up to +7.34% on LongDocURL and +5.13% on ChartCoder. So no domain is traded away for another. It also holds on every hardening strategy, and grows as the strategy demands more of the workflow: +3.57% on shared, +4.11% on paired, and +4.68% on decoy. The improvement further holds at both levels of task complexity, with multi-agent co-evolution gaining +4.31% out-of-domain at ℓ=3 and +4.09% at ℓ=5, and +5.80% and +6.21% out-of-distribution (Tab. 1). Consequently, increased task complexities does not erode the gain. Harnessing the workflow therefore improves performance across different datasets, strategies, and levels DATAWRIGHT spans, rather than on favorable subset of them. G.2 GENERALIZE THE HARNESS: OPTIMIZATION TRANSFERS TO DIFFERENT SETTINGS FLOWRIGHT generalizes to roles powered by backbones it never trains alongside. As shown in Fig. 13, powering one upstream role with Qwen3.5-4B and other roles with Qwen3.5-9B performs 28 FLOWRIGHT: It Takes Workflows to Evolve Better Workflows Figure 12: Per-Arm Results Behind the Mean Scores. Complementing the mean accuracy scores in Tab. 1, we show the accuracy (%) of each method on the 44 evaluation arms, grouped into the three in-distribution , out-of-distribution and out-of-domain . We denote the regimes (Tab. 1, D.5): hardening strategy and level as: S/P/D = Shared/Paired/Decoy, 3/5 = level. Color intensity encodes accuracy on shared scale, and hue identifies the regime. between the two single-agent baselines, gaining +11.91% over the all-4B setting when Qwen3.5-4B powers the Generator and +10.77% when Qwen3.5-4B powers the Inventor skill. Exchanging the two models reverses the result: powering the Generator and the Inventor skill with Qwen3.5-9B and the downstream agent with Qwen3.5-4B reaches 29.57%, below the all-4B baseline of 32.09%. stronger upstream model thus builds workflows for downstream agent of its own capability, which less capable downstream agent executes less effectively. Consequently, when using different backbones to power upstream and downstream roles, the downstream agent bounds what workflow performs however well it is built. Optimizing single 4B role then raises accuracy above the all-9B baseline of 47.50%, to 47.67% for the Generator, 47.96% for the Inventor skill, and 48.50% for co-evolving the two together. An optimized role transfers its gain when other roles run on different backbone it never trains with. Train-time optimization therefore generalizes across models that power the remaining roles. FLOWRIGHT improves performance whichever role it optimizes. As shown in Fig. 14, every single-role optimization outperforms the untrained baseline, and every co-evolving optimization gains more: +2.83% for the Generator, +0.90% for the Inventor skill, and +0.88% for the downstream agent alone, against +4.06% for Generator-skill co-evolution, +3.06% for upstream-downstream co-evolution, and +5.03% for multi-agent co-evolution. The Generator is the largest single lever, gaining +2.59% out-of-domain where the other two roles stay flat. The role that designs every workflow returns the largest gain among single roles. 29 FLOWRIGHT: It Takes Workflows to Evolve Better Workflows Figure 13: Roles Powered by Different Backbones. Accuracy (%) across three evaluation regimes over all 44 arms (4). Single Backbone uses one backbone for every role. Untrained Mix uses 4B or 9B backbone to specific roles, with no role optimized. Trained Role () uses the RL-trained 4B role, with Qwen3.5-9B powering other roles. Gen and Skill name the Generator and the skill it co-evolves with, and others covers every remaining role. Figure 14: Evolution of Different Roles. Accuracy (%) across three evaluation regimes over all 44 arms (4). Every role runs Qwen3.5-4B, with the only variable as which role the harness optimizes. Single-Role Self-Evolution optimizes the Generator, skill, and downstream agent individually. CoEvolution optimizes two or more together (3.4). Figure 15: Meta Distillation Across Backbones. Accuracy (%) across three evaluation regimes over all 44 arms (4). Each backbone appears as an untrained Baseline, compared with +Distill providing the meta prior distilled at five shots (3.5). 30 FLOWRIGHT: It Takes Workflows to Evolve Better Workflows Meta distillation improves every backbone, including those FLOWRIGHT never optimizes. As shown in Fig. 15, meta-distilled prior gains in all three regimes on all four backbones, and overall by +1.62% on Qwen3.5-4B, +1.53% on Qwen3.5-9B, +1.44% on GPT-5-mini, and +1.91% on GPT-5.4-mini. Every backbone keeps its weights fixed, so each gain comes from the prior alone, and GPT-5.4-mini gains most among the four. What the harness distills at test time transfers to models whose weights stay beyond reach. Optimizing the signal thus improves model FLOWRIGHT trains and model it only prompts. G.3 WEIGH THE EXECUTION: THE LADDER ADAPTS TO THE TASK TYPE Weighting execution adds the most on coding tasks. As shown in Fig. 16, an execution weight of we=0.1 improves over the untrained baselines, gaining +3.98% and +5.68% on the coding arms and +0.59% and +2.03% over all 44 arms, for Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.5-9B respectively. On coding, where workflow reaches an answer only once its code executes to earn score based on the portion of evaluation tests it passes, we=0.1 outperforms we=0.0 by +1.69% and +2.12%. Over all arms, where the answer term already covers whether workflow reaches an answer, we=0.0 leads by +2.24% and +1.86%. This is also why our main experiments hold the execution weight at 0.0 (F.1). The hierarchical ladder therefore servers as paradigm whose weights follow what each task type demands, with execution earning its own weight where the task rewards running the workflow.
